title: Celsus borrows Plato’s sun
source_text: Ἴδωμεν δὲ καὶ ἅ φησιν ἡμᾶς διδάξειν, εἰ ἄρα ἀκολουθῆσαι αὐτοῖς δυνησόμεθα, ἐν οἷς λέγει ἡμᾶς παντελῶς ἐνδεδέσθαι τῇ σαρκὶ, τοὺς, ἐὰν βιῶμεν ὀρθῶς καὶ κατὰ τὸν Ἰησοῦ λόγον, ἀκούοντας τὸ „ὑμεῖς οὐκ ἐστὲ ἐν σαρκὶ ἀλλ᾿ ἐν πνεύματι, εἴπερ πνεῦμα θεοῦ οἰκεῖ ἐν ὑμῖν.“ φησὶ δ᾿ ἡμᾶς καὶ μηδὲν καθαρὸν βλέπειν, τοὺς πειρωμένους μηδὲ μέχρι τῶν λογισμῶν ὑπὸ τῶν ἐνθυμημάτων τῆς κακίας μολύνεσθαι καὶ ἐν τῇ εὐχῇ λέγοντας· „καρδίαν καθαρὰν κτίσον ἐν ἐμοὶ ὁ θεὸς καὶ πνεῦμα εὐθὲς ἐγκαίνισον ἐν τοῖς ἐγκάτοις μου,“ ἵνα τῇ μόνῃ πεφυκυίᾳ βλέπειν θεὸν „καρδίᾳ καθαρᾷ“ θεασώμεθα αὐτόν. ἃ δὲ λέγει, τοιαῦτά ἐστιν· οὐσία καὶ γένεσις νοητὸν, ὁρατόν· μετὰ οὐσίας μὲν ἀλήθεια, μετὰ δὲ γενέσεως πλάνη. περὶ ἀλήθειαν μὲν οὖν ἐπιστήμη. περὶ δὲ θάτερον δόξα· καὶ νοητοῦ μέν ἐστι νόησις, ὁρατοῦ δὲ ὄψις. γινώσκει δὲ νοητὸν μὲν νοῦς, ὁρατὸν δὲ ὀφθαλμός. ὅπερ οὖν ἐν τοῖς ὁρατοῖς ἥλιος, οὔτ᾿ ὀφθαλμὸς ὢν οὔτ᾿ ὄψις ἀλλ᾿ ὀφθαλμῷ τε τοῦ ὁρᾶν αἴτιος καὶ ὄψει τοῦ δι᾿ αὐτὸν συνίστασθαι καὶ ὁρατοῖς τοῦ ὁρᾶσθαι, πᾶσιν αἰσθητοῖς τοῦ γίνεσθαι, καὶ μὴν αὐτὸς αὑτῷ τοῦ βλέπεσθαι, τοῦτο ἐν τοῖς νοητοῖς ἐκεῖνος, ὅσπερ οὔτε νοῦς οὔτε νόησις οὔτ᾿ ἐπιστήμη, ἀλλὰ νῷ τε τοῦ νοεῖν αἴτιος καὶ νοήσει τοῦ δι᾿ αὐτὸν εἶναι καὶ ἐπιστήμῃ τοῦ δι᾿ αὐτὸν γινώσκειν καὶ νοητοῖς ἅπασι καὶ αὐτῇ ἀληθείᾳ καὶ αὐτῇ οὐσίᾳ τοῦ εἶναι, πάντων ἐπέκεινα ὢν, ἀῤῥήτῳ τινὶ δυνάμει νοητός. ταῦτ᾿ εἴρηται μὲν ἀνθρώποις νοῦν ἔχουσιν· εἰ δέ τι αὐτῶν καὶ ὑμεῖς συνίετε. εὖ ὑμῖν ἔχει. καὶ πνεῦμα εἴ τι οἴεσθε κατιὸν ἐκ θεοῦ προαγγέλλειν τὰ θεῖα, τοῦτ᾿ ἂν εἴη τὸ πνεῦμα τὸ ταῦτα κηρύττον, οὗ δὴ πλησθέντες ἄνδρες παλαιοὶ πολλὰ κἀγαθὰ ἤγγειλαν· ὧν εἰ μὴ δύνασθε ἐπαΐειν, σιωπᾶτε καὶ τὴν ἑαυτῶν ἀμαθίαν ἐγκαλύπτετε καὶ μὴ λέγετε τυφλώττειν τοὺς βλέποντας καὶ χωλοὺς εἶναι τοὺς τρέχοντας. αὐτοὶ πάντῃ τας ψυχὰς ἀποκεχωλευμένοι καὶ ἠκρωτηριασμένοι καὶ τῷ σώματι ζῶντες, τουτέστι τῷ νεκρῷ.
pass_a_gloss: Let us see (ὁράω) also what he says he will teach (διδάσκω) us, if indeed we shall be able to follow (ἀκολουθέω) them; in which he says we are altogether bound fast (ἐνδέω) to the flesh (σάρξ), we who, if we live (βιόω) rightly and according to the word (λόγος) of Jesus, hear 'you are not in flesh but in spirit (πνεῦμα), if indeed the Spirit of God dwells (οἰκέω) in you' (Rom 8:9). And he says we see nothing pure (καθαρός), we who try (πειράομαι) not to be defiled (μολύνω) even as far as our reasonings (λογισμός) by the notions (ἐνθύμημα) of wickedness (κακία), and saying in prayer (εὐχή): 'create (κτίζω) a clean heart (καρδία καθαρά) in me, O God, and renew (ἐγκαινίζω) a right (εὐθής) spirit in my inward parts (ἔγκατα)' (LXX Ps 50:12), so that with the 'pure heart' which alone is by nature (φύω) able to see God we may behold (θεάομαι) him. What he says is of this kind [Celsus quoted]: being (οὐσία) and becoming (γένεσις): intelligible (νοητός), visible (ὁρατός). With being, truth (ἀλήθεια); with becoming, error/wandering (πλάνη). About truth, knowledge (ἐπιστήμη); about the other, opinion (δόξα). Of the intelligible, thought (νόησις); of the visible, sight (ὄψις). Mind (νοῦς) knows (γινώσκω) the intelligible, eye (ὀφθαλμός) the visible. What then the sun (ἥλιος) is among visible things, being neither eye nor sight, but cause (αἴτιος) to the eye of seeing, and to sight of its subsisting (συνίσταμαι) through it, and to visible things of being seen, to all sensibles (αἰσθητά) of coming-to-be, and indeed to itself of being beheld, this among intelligibles is that one, who is neither mind nor thought nor knowledge, but cause to mind of thinking (νοέω), and to thought of being through him, and to knowledge of knowing through him, and to all intelligibles and to truth itself and being itself of being, being beyond (ἐπέκεινα) all things, intelligible by some unspeakable (ἄρρητος) power (δύναμις). These things are said to men having mind; if you too understand (συνίημι) anything of them, it is well (εὖ ἔχει) with you. And if you think some spirit coming down (κάτειμι) from God foretells (προαγγέλλω) divine things, this would be the spirit proclaiming (κηρύσσω) these things, filled (πίμπλημι) with which ancient men (ἄνδρες παλαιοί) announced (ἀγγέλλω) many good things; which if you cannot perceive (ἐπαΐω), be silent (σιωπάω) and cover up (ἐγκαλύπτω) your own ignorance (ἀμαθία), and do not say those seeing are blind (τυφλώττω) and those running are lame (χωλός), you yourselves in every way lamed (ἀποχωλόω) and maimed (ἀκρωτηριάζω) in souls and living by the body, that is, by the dead thing (νεκρός).
pass_b_english: Let us see also what he says he will teach us, if indeed we shall be able to follow it. Here he says that we are bound fast to the flesh altogether, we who, if we live rightly and in keeping with the word of Jesus, hear the saying: “You are not in the flesh but in the Spirit, if indeed the Spirit of God dwells in you” (Romans 8:9). He says too that we see nothing pure, we who try to keep even our thoughts from being defiled by the promptings of wickedness, and who say in prayer, “Create a pure heart in me, O God, and renew a right spirit in my inmost parts” (Psalm 51:10), so that with the “pure heart” (Matthew 5:8), which alone is by nature able to see God, we may behold him.

What he says is this: “Being and becoming: the intelligible, the visible. With being goes truth; with becoming, error. Knowledge, then, is concerned with truth, and opinion with the other (compare Plato, Republic 534a; Timaeus 29c). Of the intelligible there is thought, of the visible, sight; mind knows the intelligible, and the eye the visible. What the sun is, then, among visible things, being neither eye nor sight, but the cause to the eye of its seeing, to sight of its existing through the sun, to visible things of their being seen, to all things perceived by sense of their coming into being, and indeed to itself of its being beheld, that is what he is among intelligible things, he who is neither mind nor thought nor knowledge, but is the cause to mind of its thinking, to thought of its existing through him, to knowledge of its knowing through him, and to all intelligible things, to truth itself and to being itself, of their being; he is beyond all things, and is known by the mind through a certain unspeakable power (Plato, Republic 508b-509b). These things have been said for men who have intelligence; and if you too understand any of them, it is well with you. And if you think that some spirit comes down from God to foretell divine things, this would be the spirit that proclaims these things, the spirit with which men of old were filled when they announced many good things. If you cannot grasp them, keep silent and cover up your own ignorance, and do not say that those who see are blind and that those who run are lame, when you yourselves are lamed and maimed in your souls in every way, and live by the body, that is, by what is dead.”

choices.choice: Psalm 51:10 = LXX Psalm 50:12. Celsus’s quotation runs from ‘Being and becoming’ to the end of the chapter; the full stop the source places before ‘you yourselves’ (αὐτοὶ) does not end the quotation, since Origen repeats these words of Celsus at the start of 7.46. The opening ‘bound fast to the flesh’ and ‘see nothing pure’ are Origen’s indirect reports of Celsus, so they stand without quotation marks. Celsus paraphrases Plato’s sun analogy (Republic 508b-509b, including ‘beyond being’, 509b); the being/becoming, truth/opinion pairing echoes Republic 534a and Timaeus 29c, marked ‘compare’ because Celsus does not quote either word for word. ‘ἐνθυμημάτων τῆς κακίας’ rendered ‘promptings of wickedness’. ‘ἀκολουθῆσαι αὐτοῖς’ is plural (‘them’, the things he will teach); rendered ‘it’ for English flow. ‘ζῶντες τῷ σώματι, τουτέστι τῷ νεκρῷ’: dative of means or sphere; rendered ‘live by the body, that is, by what is dead’. Celsus here speaks of ‘a spirit’ without capital: he means no Christian Holy Spirit.
Psalm 51:10 'clean heart' -> 'pure heart' so καθαρός stays one English word across Celsus's 'nothing pure', the Psalm and Matthew 5:8
'to sight of its coming to be through the sun' -> 'its existing' (συνίστασθαι; 'coming to be' is kept for γίνεσθαι later in the same sentence)
Checked: Romans 8:9, LXX Ps 50:12 = Psalm 51:10, Matthew 5:8, Republic 508b-509b, 534a, Timaeus 29c; Celsus quotation bounds correct
